segments.text: At 12 minutes past 11 on Thursday, the 12th of November, six years to the day since Jerry John Rawlings died at Korle-Bu, Kwame, the combative, dropped a grenade into the team's WhatsApp group. 19 years in power, 19 and garner still day like this.

My squad, how you dey? I am Kofi, the Editor, and this is a Gold Coast Palava Special. One man, four questions, and a chat that refused to sleep. It stands on its own, but if you have not watched our earlier editions, or our first special on Chris Hesse, the cameraman who filmed every government from Nkrumah to Rawlings, go back and watch them, because they make tonight richer. And one rule before we start, we will not worship this man, and we will not crucify him, we will weigh him.

Abba, the Restless, asked the fair question first, what exactly did he take over? On the 15th of May, 1979, a young flight lieutenant and a handful of soldiers tried to overthrow General Akufo's government and failed. He was tried, sentenced to death, and locked up. On the 4th of June, soldiers broke him out, and within hours, he was chairman of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, which ruled for 112 years.

In the last 12 days, executed eight senior officers, among them, three former heads of state, A-Chi, A-M-Pong, A-Kufo, and A-Fri-Fa, and then, on the 24th of September, handed power to the elected president, Chila Lee Mahan.
On the last day of 1981, he came back, and this time, he stayed.
Now the 1% most of us forget, 1983 hit Ghana like three storms at once.
Inflation reached 123%, the worst drought in decades dried the farms, bushfires burned what was left, and in January, Nigeria ordered illegal migrants out.
So more than a million Ghanaians came home carrying the checked bags we still call Ghana must-go.
So before anybody talks transformation, understand this.
His first job was not building a new Ghana.
It was stopping the old one from collapsing.
Kwame was not done.
Power to the people, a beg, with soldiers and curfews?
The revolution promised exactly that.

It set up peoples' and workers' defense committees in neighborhoods and workplaces, later renamed committees for the defense of the revolution, so ordinary Ghanaians could watch prices, expose corruption, and hold power to account.
But beside that, people's power sat a hard state.
Public tribunals.
MAH Kola Market demolished in the Price Control War of 1982.
And that same year, three high court judges and a retired army major were abducted and murdered, a crime that still haunts that era's memory.
Even so, the same regime set up a National Commission on Democracy to ask Ghanaians what kind of government they wanted.
And that slow conversation through the 80s is the road that eventually led to the 1992 Constitution.
The British scholar Geoffrey Haynes, who interviewed the key players over 30 years, puts it plainly.
Rawlings wanted a revolution of popular democracy, but never clearly defined the new system and lacked the ideological and institutional capacity to build it.
He was brilliant at pulling an old order down and far less sure what to put in its place.
Yet one piece did survive.
In 1988, his government created 110 district assemblies, two-thirds of their members elected, and the assembly in your own district today is a grandchild of that law.
Baba, the ascendant, spotted the contradiction that every serious study of this man wrestles with.
How does a revolutionary who came to fight the old order end up with the IMF and the World Bank?
In April 1983, with the country starving, the government launched the economic recovery program.
Deep devaluation, price controls lifted, state firms trimmed, and foreign money flowing in.
By the World Bank's figures, inflation fell from 123% in 1983 to 40% in 1986 and 18% by 1991.
And the economy grew by about 5% a year, until Ghana became the West's favorite example of adjustment that worked.
And remember how far we had fallen.
At independence in 1957, Ghana's income per head stood at about the level of South Korea's.
And by 1983, we were queuing for basic essentials.
Was that a rescue or a retreat?
Both.
The shelves filled, but urban workers swallowed the pain,
and the dream of a self-reliant people's economy quietly gave way to a market economy run by a soldier.
Kevin Shillington, writing in 1992 as Ghana prepared for the Fourth Republic,
asked how real that recovery felt to the ordinary Ghanaian.
Three decades on, the question still stands.
Then, Amo, the discerning, who had Abba reading the whole chat to him,
asked the question this special exists for.
One witness is Kwa Mehna Ahwoi,
who worked beside Rawlings from the PNDC into the NDC years,
and published Working with Rawlings in 2020.
He calls him a born leader with a mesmerizing charisma,
but writes that Rawlings had no plan and no strategy on how to materially develop Ghana,
and that in meetings he sometimes looked out of the window or played with his toy planes
while technical matters were debated.
Rawlings' office replied that the book was generously economical with the truth
and rejected many of its claims.
So take it as one insider's account, not the final word.
There is also the trap of success.
The outsider became the establishment.
He won the 1992 election with about 60%,
and when the opposition boycotted the parliamentary vote,
his party took almost every seat.
In 1995, when crowds marched against the new VAT under the cry of Kume Preko,
four people were shot dead by unidentified gunmen.
He won again in 1996 with 57% against Kufwar's 40,
and then, crucially, he obeyed the two-term limit.
Here is the irony.
On the 7th of January, 2001, he handed power to John Kufwar,
the first peaceful transfer from a sitting government to the opposition in our history.
And Kufwar had once served about eight months as a secretary
in Rawlings' own first PNDC government.
A move Achwoi says was partly about keeping Nigeria's president,
Shaga Ri, a friend of Kufwar's, on side for oil.
Close to half past one, Abba asked for a verdict,
and Achwoi himself gave me the best one,
an old Akan proverb about the nightjar bird.
Santro fi ano ma, wo che no a, wa che mamu su o,
wo jaye no a, wa jaye ade.
Catch it and you have caught a curse.
Let it go and you have let go of something precious.
That is the man in one line.
The revolutionary who did not finish his revolution,
the pragmatist who pulled Ghana back from collapse,
the strong man who still gave us the constitution,
the term limits and the handover that made our democracy.
So here is the lesson squad.
Anger can diagnose a nation but only a plan can heal it
and 19 years of power cannot replace one good blueprint.
Now it is your turn.
If you had to fill that ledger,
which column carries more weight for you,
the curse or the precious thing, and why?
Write it in the comments and let us argue like a family,
with facts and with respect.
This has been a Gold Coast Pallava special.
We will meet you back at the nest.
Cheers.
